blocks.x: Okay, we got it on again. This is Zeno. We're back interviewing you.
So used to him. I'm so used to him. It's just like George to me.
The last time you were talking, you asked if you should speak in French. Would you rather talk in French than English usually?
Well, I have to talk in English, you know, because it's only English now. Yeah, I prefer French. Oh yes. Give me my language.
Do you still read very much or not?
Well, I can't read no more, Mr. Russell.
Because of your eyes now. Now where are all of your books? Are they still over at your other home? All of your books that you had?
They fall over there. They're over there. Piles and piles and piles of books.
Did you read very much when you were young?

I'd get in the bed. It had candles then, you know. Yes, by candlelight. Candle. I'd get under the mosquito bar with the candle and I'd read my mom and say, Oh, that girl gonna set this house afire. She'd read, Oh, I loved to read when I was young. But not foolishness, no. I never read foolishness.
All serious good books.
Yes, I never liked foolishness. Did you read?
You don't have to look at me, you just go ahead and talk. No, we'll just be talking is alright. Did you read mostly French books or um? French. French.
French. What do you say, Mitch? Oh, that's...
I'm sorry. Well, that's... That's a... I'm sorry. That's a bright light. Did that bother you? No, it scared me. Scared you?
Well, it'll go off every once in a while. Oh, I thought you'd be used to that by now. I oughta be. So many camera people around. Oh.

All the time. I had people in that little 2x4 room. Taking pictures up there, yeah, so many. Um, did that hurt your eyes? No, I run water, you know, all the time. You're just scared, that's all. Because, uh... No, my eyes run water because I'm so young, you know, I'm 94 years old. I don't believe it. Well, you're very polite indeed. You don't believe it. Viscuit au croix, vous serez venir m'encher?
You have to talk to his wife. Eh? His wife speaks French. Not him. I'd like to see her.
Maybe that won't bother you so much over there. Put it over here. Then you won't have to look at it.
Eh?
Yeah, so don't be, don't be surprised when it goes off there again.
Well, I oughta be used to that.
Yes. Well, you didn't know there would be a bright light right there. I had it too close to you, I think.
This time it won't be close. Yes. What was your favorite book of all? Hmm? What was your favorite book of all? Your favorite book?

Well, I read everything that was good. Everything that could open my intelligence. Oh, I see. I never read foolishness. Never did love stories and all that. I never did care about that. I like serious things. Now, you see, I tried to follow La Vie, La Fille, Jean La Fille. Oh, yeah. And I had a big bundle of, you know, out of the newspaper. Oh, yeah. My mom said she's gonna go crazy. She burned him up.
Did you read anything in Spanish or German books too?
She thought reading would drive you crazy?
She thought so. I ain't crazy. She's gone. I'm 94 years. I ain't crazy. I'm a long ways from being crazy, yes.
Helped your mind to read those.
I love to read. Oh, I love good literature.
And was, Bill says, was French the only language you could read in?

Well, it's the language that I could read with more facilité, you know. Yes. But I read because, you see, old Mrs. W. W. King, Grace King. Her mother? Huh? Grace King's mother? Grace King's mother. I worked there. And there they used to have classes every three, about four days in the week. One day it would be Capitán de Chivarria, that was for the Spanish. And nothing but Spanish. And they speak it to me and I dig it like a little young crazy thing, you know. I wasn't twenty years old. Then one day it was Herman Gassner. You must have, Herman Gassner, he teaches at Hueline. But this Herman Gassner that's there, must be his grandson. But old Herman Gassner used to teach at Miss King, Capitaine de Chivarria, Miss Guigar, Madame Gérard, and, how do you call them? Charles Guayari.
And which language did Guayari teach?
French, with Madame Gérard.

Who was that lady that was voted, you know, she got some honor about two years ago, that she was voted the best teacher of the year. Do you remember she sent you her orchids that time? Do you remember she? I don't remember.
She got some award.
Was she from Newcomb? From Newcomb, yes. Could that be her?
Gracie K, Gracie, Ranshaw, Gladys Ranshaw. That's who it was, Gladys Ranshaw. Gladys Ranshaw, yes.
And you worked for them too, did you? So the more born. I don't remember the lady, how she looked.
Maybe she don't teach no more now. No, she's retired, I guess. Retired.
But you worked for them then too, did you?
I've been in that family since her sister, which is dead now, was 14 years old.
Is she related to Miss LeBreton? Huh? Is she related to Miss LeBreton? Who? Gladys Ranshaw?
Well, that's her sister. I see.
Yes.

George Ranshaw had, I believe, nine girls and two boys. Ah, but that was a man. Worth imitating. He had such nice manners, so quiet, so serious, so charitable. Oh, I liked the judge very much. Stayed with him till he left this earth.

I was wondering if you could tell us any more about your grandmother. If you remember more about her. You told us a little bit about her the other day. How she taught you some of these Senegalese, Senegal words. Did she teach you some of the songs too? Yeah.
Did she teach you to sing? No, she never taught me many songs. Just that was sung of Haiti. All Haitians, since 11 years old, have suffered from the most miserable. How was that?
Did that bother you?
You want to blind me, I see.
No, I pointed it at the wall. Oh, yeah. It sounded good.

No. But she speak to me. I was only one she speak her language too. Because my mother didn't want to go talk that with Alice. Don't come to me with that. Go talk that with Alice. And I loved it. I followed every step she made. And I'd ask her. Again, show me. Tell me. Yes, tell me.
And what were some of the expressions she taught you from Senegal?

Well, Abadra, that means good for nothing. Abadra is good for nothing. And good morning, Salikum, everybody, Serum. Salikum, Serum, that's good morning everybody. And at night, Balikum, Serum. And how's everybody home? Pelemete, Dumbaya, Kayaka.
And what did she call the puddings? What did she call the pudding that you made?
Pepe-pate.
Yes, pepe-pate.
Well, that's French. Yes, pepe-pate is French.
That was that sweet potato pudding.
Made great. Not boiled, no. Grate. You grate it? And you put plenty of black pepper in it.
Oh, really hot then, is it?
I didn't like it much on account of that pepe-pate, that black pepper, you know? Yes. And she used to make funny dishes, you know, her home dish.
What other kind of dishes did they have?
Red beans with bananas.
Oh, red beans and bananas. That sounds good to me. I like both of them.

I like it. I like all the galamacha, as my mom called it. All what my grandmother cooked. It was fine. Where did red beans and bananas come from? From Senegal. That's a Senegal dish. And what are some of the other Senegal dishes? Well, they had tum tum. And that is? Tum tum is okra cooked with sweet potato, but the white sweet potato. That's tum tum.
And did they make gumbo in Senegal, or do you know? Yes, they made gumbo. What kind of gumbo would they make? Well, okra.
Okra, the country you know.
Yes.
They make tum tum. Both okra and gumbo are African words. Did you know that?
Yes.
They're both African words.

Well, my grandmother used to cook it. And she'd fried bananas with ham. I miss my grandmother. I wish she was over a hundred when she died, so I know she'd be just like a monkey now. But I miss her. I miss her.
You lived over on St. Claude Street in those days, was it?
St. Claude? There we all was born. My grandmother had 13 or 23 grandchildren. All born on St. Claude, between Calarec and Columbus. All born right there in that house.
You went to that church over on St. Claude, what is the name of this?
St. Augustine. St. Augustine. St. Claude and Governor Nicholas, they call it now. Used to be called by road. Now they call it Governor Nicholas.
And where were you married? Were you married in that church?
No, St. Joseph.
And on Tulane Street? Yes. I was told you then, Bill, when we passed by.
It wasn't built. It wasn't complete. It just had start building it. They didn't have no windows, no confessional bars, no nothing. Okay? When I married there.

I wanted to ask you about a dance. Did you ever hear of a dance called the Kalenda? Kalenda? Kalenda. Oh yes. And how was that dance? That's a Creole dance. I see. Would they dance in couples or alone or? No, dance alone. They'd hold a dress like that, you know. Oh. They'd dress.
Hold up the dress that way, you know.
And they'd dance alone. Would the woman or man do it, or both?

Well, nobody danced together. They didn't dance together like now. They danced by themselves. Well, that's a Senegal pattern too. And then they used to sing. I remember now just . . . . 된 stuff with They set all up. They didn't have music like they got now, you see, in my grandmother's time. They didn't have music, they sing. Sing all the time and dance. They didn't have music.
They sing by themselves, no instruments though.
No, no, no instruments. They sing and dance.
When did they start dancing in couples and in fours?

Oh, well I don't remember that because you see when I began to have age of reason they was already dancing. Yes, La Cachute is a Spanish dance. They would dance it together. And so from there, that would dance together. They hold their arm like that and they just make steps like that. So from there, that's a Spanish dance.

Yes. I was wondering about several things. Do you remember when they had the battle on Canal Street? At the foot of Canal? Mm-hmm. That was years and years ago. You may have just been a little girl then. Yes, I must have been. But that was during the reconstruction days.
I must have been very young then. Yes.
You know, they had federal troops here. Do you remember when they had the federal troops?
troops after the war? I think they had until she was about 12 years old maybe 1877 was it or something?
until 77 it was. I think that's when the battle was in 77. You should have been about 12 years old. It's funny you didn't remember any
Well you see, children didn't go about like the children now. You couldn't pick yourself and go where you want.
Did you ever get uptown up to Canal Street very often when you were a girl? No, not often. I'd go with my grandmother

because I followed her every step she made and she'd tell me, Toa Sa, c'est la rue du Canal. And then when she passed on Esplanade Street she'd tell me, c'est l'esplanade. And they had an old house I remember on that side of the banquet. Old brick house, the brick would fall like dust you know. And she told me, you see, toa Sa, c'est la niga tre da.
Is that on Esplanade? That was on Esplanade.

What was that last word? Niga tre da. Where they sold niggers. Where they trade. Oh, like trading. So you see, she's being so Frenchy. And me too. She said niga tre da. Now, had she ever been in Haiti? My grandmother? Yes. No, her mother was told from her. She was not in Haiti. She was in Senegal.
Yes.
Haiti is somewhere in Cuba, between Cuba and Spain. Yeah. North.
Well, I just wondered, you sang that song, you know, which dealt with the revolution down there. And I just wondered if she'd...
Well, you see, my grandmother used to sing it to me all the time. That's how I could...
I wondered where she learned it.
From her mother.
Oh, from her mother.

Because her mother came there and was told from her country, you see. When she says... She said he was eight years old. But she couldn't speak nothing. But they had an old man at Charles Perrette. That bought all the Senegalian niggers that he could. And an old man they called Pajaco. And he was a Senegalian. And he translated, you know. And that's where my great-grandmother then began to learn how to speak. But she said she was eight years old. And they had gone to bed by the... By the... Not lagume. Lagume is Spanish. By the river anyhow. Yes. And she said they saw a man. And he had pretty things in his hand. And that must have been red beads and things, you know, like that. And he made them come to get. And that's how they brought her. Yeah. She was only eight years old. My grandmother.
My great-grandmother. And she remembered them. When the slave traders came there.
And stuff like

what I gotta eat, gris, mashed potatoes, anything like I can't eat meat no more. Well you're healthy though. Well I ought not to complain because from my age I see many younger than me that is more helpless than I am. Well and you enjoy
life though don't you? You still enjoy life. Oh yes. If I was over

there on St. Philip Street my old two by four I'd be fixing my thing my windows and can't climb no more to put coisins but I'd pay somebody to hang up my couldn't fix Christmas. Gladys Rancho every time she comes she say well at least you still have the spirit as I'm gonna have it till I die. That's good. You mentioned about the very very very song. Oh yes I like like to make Santa Claus like to make the Santa Claus for the children you know who I love to all that St. Philip Street. What
was Christmas like when you were a girl did they have any big celebration trees or

anything? Oh yes they had tree no they didn't have trees that I can remember but the old folks would take a high something you know something high enough and they didn't have all the little lights and things like they didn't have things like they got now and the dolls wasn't like now the body was sawdust and this part was just and just half of the arms you know yeah all the rest was sawdust. Like rag dolls I guess. And rag dolls yes they make plenty rag dolls my grandmother used to make

rag dolls for all of us. I was wondering a little bit about the George's early life we didn't get to talk so much to George the other time. No. When he first took up his clarinet and started playing you mentioned you taught him one little song was that on his little flute or on his clarinet? No on the flute. On the flute. How long did he play that

flute before he took his clarinet? He wanted the clarinet you know and George was always small and I thought George wouldn't live to see 15 years I didn't want to give. I said I'll give you a violin but I'll not give you a clarinet because you'll die before you're 15 years old. And he oh no more I don't want no violin I want a clarinet. Well I never did give it to him until one day he asked I sent him to bring because I used to wash plenty shirts and more so. I sent him to bring a basket of clothes by Mr. Grima on St. Louis Street. I had sent him around the corner to bring some clothes and I gave him a nickel I believe a nickel or a dime I don't remember. When he come back I said well now go bring Mr. Edgar Grima's clothes or shirts and collars. They wore collars the tash. Oh yes I did too. Yeah. And he said Mo can I get can I get a flute? I said no thank you George I just gave you I don't remember it was a nickel or a dime. He said it only cost a dime. I said go ahead and get it. And he went and he got that little ten cents flute and that's where he started. Tululu, And I never never give him a clarinet. And one day he went with his father on Canal Street and was looking in the showcase and he told his papa you see I want that and mama don't want to give it to me. And his father said well let's go and get and see. So he went inside and Mr. the clerk told him it's for this little fella. He told him yes. He said well I he's a beginner I have a small one second hand I suppose but it's forty dollars. For a beginner it's all right. And that's where he went he started that's where he started with the clarinet. But I never give him no clarinet.
How old was George's father when he when he died? We were 10 years. How old was George?
Well Henry's dead now. My my grandson dead above Joseph. It's 34 years ago. Because he was under Joseph was under six months I believe when his grandfather died.
Yeah well when did George change his name to Lewis? When was that? Well I don't remember the year. I mean about how old was he? Was he playing

music then and changed it? Well he'd play at night you know. He was working on the river. And twice he got hurted on the river and didn't know. And he belonged to the national insurance. Yes. Because I had all my children in the national. And I had them George uh uh uh uh uh Joseph Lewis Zeno. And him but everybody called him George Lewis. So that name went on so that made a confusion. So the man told him you'll have to do that either one or the other. That's why he went to the notary I believe.
And just let it be George Lewis. They called him that down on the river front too. Yes. That name. I thought maybe he changed it on account of music.
No no. To have an easier name you know. No no. It was just by having so much trouble with the insurance. Insurance. He just let it go George Lewis short. But all his children and his wife and
and how did you pronounce his first name originally was it Francois or how do you?
Joseph Francis. Joseph Francis.
Oh Joseph Francis. Yes. I forgot how.
Well everybody call him George. My my mother say call him George he'll be good.
Well I can't complain. No that's a good name. It's easy to remember. It's easier to remember and say it that way.

You see I had lost already three children before I raised George. And I was so outdone, so discouraged. I was losing my mind. So when George came, my mother said, Peleli George, he live. I said, well that's, we called him George. But he wasn't christened George.
Did he practice much around the house? Was he always bothering you playing a lot?

All day, all day when he wasn't at school. He was with that clarinet, that clarinet. Put his head at the foot of the bed and his foot on the heading of the bed. And that toodaloo, toodaloo all day long. The day of the storm, I thought, sure we would all perish. I believe it was 18, 1915, eh? I think 1915. That it swept almost the city. All day, I was there, I was afraid to iron. I was afraid of lightning. And I kept telling him, George, prepare your soul. We may all be in judgment before the day is out. And he kept on with that music, kept on with that. And about six o'clock, that's the last, the wind passed through the house. I was the only one in the house. All the slates and everything had gone. And the house looked like the house was crumbling. And he run to me and he put his head, I said, prepare your soul. It's all.
It was a bad storm, I guess. I read about it.
Oh, that was a storm. And he told me that they have worse storms than that, but that's about the worst one I saw.
Do you remember any of the big floods when you were a girl? Was there water in the houses?

Plenty, plenty of water. Plenty, plenty. See, they didn't have no sewage. The Kong, what do they call it, Kong? Blind Eel, I believe they called them. Big, big moccasins or something like that. Oh, yes. Yeah, they're poisonous. But sometimes the water would come to the door and then things would get out of the door. What's the name? And come in the house.
Water moccasins. Moccasins, I believe.
Water moccasins. Yeah. We called them Kong in French.
What kind of pieces did George play when he was a boy?
Everything he heard. Everything he heard. He practiced and tried and make a mistake and come back until he played right.

pretty costumes? No they didn't have no pretty costumes in the Mardi Gras my days. They masked, some would mask and plenty Indians but they dressed like the Indian. They didn't no fancy thing. My cousin Tati which would be 89 years old now in March, he used to have a gang, his band you know. It was really amusing.
Were there many instruments out in the street? Any bands that you remember? No.

If they had bands it was young people you know. Some had tin plates and spoons. They'd hit on that band. Some had washboard and they'd make music with that. What would they hit the washboard with? Well I don't know what they'd do but they'd have the washboard and they'd run the hand like this on it you know. And make music.
